best_text:
The original formulation of the theory of relativity (special relativity) included a postulate: the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the light source. This postulate, which has since been experimentally verified, has profound consequences for our understanding of space and time. In particular, it implies that space and time are not independent entities, but are instead interwoven in a four-dimensional fabric called spacetime. Furthermore, it implies that the laws of physics are the same for all observers in uniform motion relative to one another (the principle of relativity), and it unites time with the three dimensions of space into a single continuum known as spacetime. Events that occur at the same time for one observer will occur at different times for another if the observers are in relative motion.
The theory of relativity has two parts: special relativity and general relativity. Special relativity applies to all physical phenomena in the absence of gravity. General relativity explains the law of gravitation and its relation to other forces of nature. It applies to the cosmological and astrophysical realm, including astronomy.
